passages.happening:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘I will bring upon Pharaoh and Egypt one more plague. After that, he will allow you to leave this place. And when he lets you go, he will drive you out completely’” (verse 1).

The people are to ask their neighbors for silver and gold (verse 2). “And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover, Moses himself was highly regarded in Egypt by Pharaoh’s officials and by the people” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
This chapter is a hinge. The nine plagues are over. The Passover and the leaving have not yet begun. In between, the last blow is announced.

Chapter 10 ended with Pharaoh banishing Moses, and Moses agreeing never to see his face again. Yet in verses 4 to 8 Moses is still speaking to Pharaoh. Most readers take verses 1 to 3 as a step aside, telling what God had already said to Moses, and verses 4 to 8 as the rest of Moses' last speech in that same meeting. Only in verse 8 does he finally walk out.

The command to ask for silver and gold was given first at the burning bush (3:21-22). Older English Bibles said ‘borrow’, which made Israel look dishonest. The Hebrew simply means ‘ask’. And the text says the Egyptians gave because the LORD gave Israel favor with them. Many readers see it as wages long overdue for generations of unpaid work.

Notice verse 3. Moses was ‘highly regarded’ among Pharaoh's officials and the Egyptian people. Ordinary Egyptians did not all share their king's hardness.
passages.later:
God had promised Abraham that his family would come out of slavery “with many possessions” (Genesis 15:14).

Israel's law turned this into a rule for every freed slave: “And when you release him, do not send him away empty-handed” (Deuteronomy 15:13). The reason given is this very memory: “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 15:15).

The gold had a mixed future. The people later gave gold for the tabernacle (Exodus 35:22), but gold earrings also went into the golden calf (Exodus 32:2-4). The same gifts could serve God's worship or be made into an idol.
passages.asks: The gold of Egypt could be given to God or made into an idol. Ask what gifts and resources God has put in your hands. And ask whether you are using them for his worship, or shaping them into something you trust in his place.

passages.happening:
“So Moses declared, ‘This is what the LORD says: ‘About midnight I will go throughout Egypt, and every firstborn son in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the servant girl behind the hand mill, as well as the firstborn of all the cattle’’” (verses 4-5).

“Then a great cry will go out over all the land of Egypt. Such an outcry has never been heard before and will never be heard again” (verse 6). But among the Israelites, “not even a dog will snarl at man or beast” (verse 7).

Pharaoh's officials will bow before Moses and say, “Go, you and all the people who follow you!” (verse 8). “And hot with anger, Moses left Pharaoh’s presence.”
passages.hearers:
This is the last plague, and it is the one God warned about before the contest began. At the start God told Moses to say to Pharaoh, ‘Israel is My firstborn son’, and that if Pharaoh would not let God's son go, his own firstborn would die (4:22-23). Pharaoh had ordered Israel's sons thrown into the Nile (1:22). Now the judgment turns back on Egypt's sons.

The firstborn son was the family's heir, the sign of its future. Pharaoh's firstborn was the crown prince, heir to a throne Egyptians thought divine. The last plague strikes every house at the point of its greatest hope.

Verse 5 covers the whole of Egyptian society, from the palace to the lowest servant. Grinding grain by hand, kneeling at a stone and pushing a smaller stone over it, was daily drudgery given to the lowest household servants. Egyptian figurines show women at that very work.

‘A great cry’ uses the same Hebrew word as Israel's cry under slavery, the cry God heard at the bush (3:7, 9). Now the oppressor cries as the oppressed once cried.

‘Not even a dog will snarl’ is in Hebrew, word for word, that not a dog will sharpen its tongue. It means complete calm. On the night every Egyptian house is wailing, Israel's houses will be so quiet that not even a dog barks. This is the last time the book says God ‘makes a distinction’ between them.

Moses leaves ‘hot with anger’. The text does not tell us all he felt. But he has given the warning that will cost Egypt its children, and Pharaoh still would not listen.
passages.later:
God takes no delight in this. Through Ezekiel he asks, “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD. Wouldn’t I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23).

God's word about life and death is spoken in Deuteronomy: “I bring death and I give life; I wound and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39).

The New Testament speaks of Jesus as God's firstborn in a new way. He is “the beginning and firstborn from among the dead” (Colossians 1:18), the first to rise into the new creation. And God “did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). Paul's words there echo Abraham and Isaac more than Exodus, but Christians see the two stories meet at the cross.
passages.hard:
How can a just God kill the firstborn children of Egypt? This is the hardest moment in the plague story, and the text does not soften it. It announces the death of every firstborn, from the palace to the servant's quarters, and it records the great cry that follows. Readers who doubt the events happened as told still face the question of what the story says about God.

Several things are said in response. First, the judgment answers a crime. Pharaoh had ordered the killing of Israel's newborn sons (1:16, 22), and God warned him before the first plague that refusing to release God's firstborn would cost him his own (4:22-23). Nine plagues and months of warnings came first. Second, Scripture presents God, the giver of life, as having an authority over life and death that no human being has. The Bible never offers this plague as a model for human violence. Third, Israel's firstborn were not spared for being innocent. They too were under the sentence and were protected only by the blood of the Passover lamb (12:13), and afterward God claimed them as his own (13:2). Christians add that the story does not end with God taking the firstborn of others, but with God giving up his own Son.

None of these answers takes away the grief of the text, and thoughtful Christians admit that it remains a place where they must trust what they cannot fully see. Jewish tradition has grieved for Egypt too. The Talmud tells that God silenced the angels who wanted to sing as the Egyptians drowned, saying that the work of his hands was dying. The Bible tells of judgment soberly, and it does not ask anyone to rejoice in a child's death.

Behind every one of those Egyptian doors was a mother. If you have lost a child, or carry a grief like hers, please do not carry it alone. Speak to someone you trust, a pastor or a grief counsellor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The cry of Egypt's mothers was the same word as the cry of Israel's slaves. Ask what it means to you that God hears every cry, even the cry of those who were on the wrong side. And ask whether you can hold together the justice of God and real grief for those who suffer under it.

passages.t: The wonders multiplied, and Pharaoh's heart hardened
passages.happening:
“The LORD said to Moses, ‘Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that My wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt’” (verse 9).

“Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, but the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart so that he would not let the Israelites go out of his land” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
These two verses close the whole run of plagues. They repeat what God said at the start, in 7:3-4: he would multiply his signs and wonders, and Pharaoh would not listen. The cycle is framed by that promise and its keeping. Nothing that happened took God by surprise.

The verse says again that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart. The chapter notes on Exodus 4 and 9 set out the main ways Christians read this, and why these notes take no side.
passages.later:
God's words at the start of the plagues are the frame for this verse: “But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and though I will multiply My signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, Pharaoh will not listen to you” (Exodus 7:3-4).

Paul writes in Romans 9 that God “hardens whom He wants to harden” (Romans 9:18), and in the same letter he calls the reader to wonder rather than to judge: “O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33).
passages.asks: The plagues end where they began, with God's word kept. Ask what it means to you that nothing in this long, hard story took God by surprise. And ask whether you can trust him with parts of your own story you do not yet understand.
